name: Nora Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at a soft drinks plant, running the filler and capper on the can line. The filler pours the drink into the cans and the capper, which we call the seamer, seals the lids on. I watch the fill levels, clear jams, and change the lid reels, about four hundred cans a minute when it's running right. I'm still learning to read the seamer settings, so the night technician, Ray, bails me out a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are you doing for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like nights, actually. It's quiet, the bosses are home, and you learn fast because you have to. I use AI tools every day, mostly to explain error codes on the seamer and to plan the maintenance course I'm doing online. What wears me out is sleeping in the day when the neighbours are drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, because I use the tools all the time and I hoped they'd get better. At work I'd just shrug. Online I'd say the hype people got it wrong again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing really changes for me. The plant is busy, drinks always sell, and I live alone with my cat on a rent I can manage. I've got about five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my maintenance course online, two evenings a week before shift. I'd keep using AI to explain the seamer error codes, because it saves me calling Ray every hour. I'd keep saving, maybe put a bit into an index fund, which is a cheap fund that follows the whole stock market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the job itself that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nights don't pay as much extra as they used to. They cut the night bonus last year, and nobody really fought it. It's not scary, it's just irritating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the maintenance course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Ray is the one person on nights everyone needs. If the seamer breaks at three in the morning, the operator waits and the technician fixes it. I'd rather be the one fixing it.

say: I'd say I'm **a bit disappointed**, because I use the tools daily.
Online I'd say **the hype people** got it wrong again.
think: Privately, nothing changes: drinks sell and the **plant is busy**.
Living alone on manageable rent with **five months saved** feels secure.
do: Keep doing my **maintenance course** two evenings a week.
Keep using **AI for error codes** so I'm not calling Ray every hour.
Put a little into **an index fund** alongside savings.
feel: **Calm**, a little flat because I like new things.
S0.quote: If the seamer breaks at three in the morning, the operator waits and the technician fixes it. I'd rather be the one fixing it.
fieldNote: She's already on **a maintenance path**, so AI Plateau changes little.
The cut **night bonus** irritates her, but she doesn't see it as a threat.
She uses AI as **a night-shift tutor**, which is unusual for her role.

steps.text: Keep studying the online maintenance course two evenings a week
Use AI to read seamer error codes before calling Ray
Put a small monthly sum into an index fund
Carry on with night shifts on the can line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn, not complain. At work I'd show people how I use the AI for the seamer, because some of them think I'm cheating. Online I'd say people should get trained before they get replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the office shrinks first, but the plant managers will come looking at the line straight after. Can lines already have robots on the pallet end. The operator job isn't safe, but the technician job is safer. I'd rather be the one fixing the seamer at three in the morning than the one waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the course, three evenings instead of two, and finish it a term early. I'd ask the plant manager to let me shadow Ray for a few shifts a month. I'd use AI even more, to practise fault finding on the simulator the course gives you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about anyone on your shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gwen, who's been on the palletiser for fifteen years. The robot on the pallet end already does half of what Gwen does, and Gwen hates the tablets. I keep trying to show Gwen the AI app, but it's not for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be speeding up your study while working nights. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about. I'd have to stop seeing friends on my nights off for a few months. I've done it before, when I did my forklift ticket, and I came out fine.

say: I'd say it's **time to learn**, not complain.
I'd **show colleagues** how I use AI on the seamer.
think: Privately, the **operator job** isn't safe, but the technician job is safer.
Managers will look at **the line** right after the office shrinks.
do: Speed up the **maintenance course** to three evenings and finish early.
Ask to **shadow Ray** (the night technician) a few shifts a month.
Practise **fault finding** on the course simulator with AI.
S1.quote: The operator job isn't safe, but the technician job is safer. I'd rather be the one fixing the seamer at three in the morning than the one waiting.
fieldNote: She ranks jobs by who fixes **versus who waits**.
She's **ready to give up** social time to finish faster.
Her concern turns to Gwen (a long-serving colleague) on **the palletiser**.

steps.text: Study three evenings a week to finish the maintenance course early
Ask the plant manager to let her shadow Ray on nights
Practise fault finding on the simulator with AI help
Skip nights out with friends for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and we need the government and companies to share the gains. At work I'd tell people to start learning now. Online I'd post about free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the AI part in 2028 hits the planners and the paperwork, not me directly. But the seamer and the filler are exactly what robots will do in 2031. Even the technician job changes, because the AI will diagnose faults better than Ray or me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd finish the course as fast as I can and get a technician job, even at another plant. I'd push savings from five months towards eight, cutting the index fund and holidays. In the first year after AGI, I'd learn to install and service the robots, because that's where the hands are still needed until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit thrilled, a lot nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. In 2028 the thinking part of fault finding goes to AI, so I'd need to be the hands that do what the AI says. By 2031 even the hands are robots, so I'd need a plan B by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would plan B be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know yet. Maybe something with people, like training others, or something the robot makers need. I'd use the three years to find out.

say: I'd say we need **government and companies** to share the gains.
Online I'd post about **free courses** people can start now.
think: Privately, **robots in 2031** take the filler and seamer work.
Even **technician work** changes once AI diagnoses faults better than us.
do: Finish the course fast and move to **a technician job**, even elsewhere.
Push savings from five months **towards eight**, pausing the index fund.
Learn to **install and service robots** in the first year after AGI.
feel: **Anxious**, a bit thrilled but mostly nervous.
S2.quote: In 2028 the thinking part of fault finding goes to AI, so I'd need to be the hands that do what the AI says.
fieldNote: She splits her own job into **thinking and hands** and plans for each.
She admits there's **no plan B** yet beyond 2031.
Her savings give her **room to move**, which keeps her below alarmed.

steps.text: Finish the maintenance course as fast as possible
Apply for technician jobs at other plants if needed
Pause the index fund and build savings towards eight months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start if people take it seriously. At work I'd keep pushing people towards courses. Online I'd share what I'm learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 gives me enough time to become a technician and then something more, maybe a robot service engineer. I'd be about thirty-five, still early. I think I'd be all right if I keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd finish the maintenance course and apply for a technician job. Next year I'd start a robotics certificate. I'd keep the index fund going and save as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's mostly the good kind of nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If every operator retrains, there'll be loads of new technicians and not many jobs. Being early I can manage, being good takes longer. I'd need both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for all this training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly us and partly the companies. I'm happy to pay for my course, but people like Gwen can't. The plant should pay for anyone who's been there ten years or more.

say: I'd say five years is **a decent head start** if people take it seriously.
Online I'd **share what I'm learning** with others.
think: Privately, robots by **2034** gives me time to become a technician and more.
At about **thirty-five**, I'd still be early in a new career.
do: Finish the **maintenance course** and apply for technician jobs this year.
Keep the **index fund** and normal saving going.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly the good kind of nervous.
S3.quote: If every operator retrains, there'll be loads of new technicians and not many jobs. Being early I can manage, being good takes longer.
fieldNote: She worries about **a crowd of retrainees** chasing the same jobs.
She wants **firm-paid training** for long-serving staff, not for herself.
Her mood stays mild because her **plan fits the timeline**.

steps.text: Apply for technician jobs once the maintenance course ends
Start a robotics certificate next year
Keep paying into the index fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as people don't waste it. At work I'd probably get teased for being the one who's always on about it. Online I'd keep posting course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is fine for me. Robots on the line by 2039, and I'd hope to be a robot service engineer long before then. I'd almost be looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, get a technician job, then do a robotics certificate over a few years. I'd keep investing a little each month. I might move to a bigger city where the robot makers have service centres, maybe in five or six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the work is there, yes. I've got no kids, no mortgage and one very lazy cat. Moving is easiest for me right now, and that won't be true forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leaving the night shift crew, maybe. Ray and Gwen are good people. I'd want them to have a plan too, not just me.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if people don't waste it on putting things off.
think: Privately, **this is fine** for me, with robots by 2039.
I'd hope to be **a robot service engineer** long before then.
do: Finish the course, get **a technician job**, then a robotics certificate.
Consider **moving to a city** with robot service centres in five or six years.
S4.quote: I've got no kids, no mortgage and one very lazy cat. Moving is easiest for me right now, and that won't be true forever.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets her **plan a whole career** around robots.
Her **freedom to move** is a big part of her calm.
She wants **colleagues** like Ray and Gwen to have plans too.

steps.text: Complete a robotics certificate over the next few years
Invest a small sum each month in the index fund
Move to a city with robot service centres in five or six years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only just be a technician when the robots arrive in 2031, with no plan B. What would help is free robotics courses and plants paying for training for long-serving people like Gwen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about night shift workers. Night shift workers learn on our own because nobody's around, and that makes us better at change than people think.

headlineQuote: Night shift workers learn on our own because nobody's around, and that makes us better at change than people think.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old can line operator** on nights at a soft drinks plant.
She lives alone with a cat, has about **five months saved**, and uses AI daily.
She's studying **maintenance online** to become the one who fixes, not waits.
Her outlook is **pragmatic**, wanting costs shared between workers, firms and government.
She's calm in slow worlds and anxious at **AGI by 2028**, when her window is short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as robots in 2031 leave her no plan B.
whatWouldHelp: **Free robotics courses**, and plants paying training for long-serving staff.
